title: Polynomials in an Operator
---

When the domain and codomain of a linear map coincide, we gain additional algebraic structure: the ability to compose maps with themselves. Recall from Chapter 5 that a linear map $\varphi : V \to V$ is a *linear operator*, or *endomorphism*, of $V$, and that $\End(V) = \Hom(V, V)$ is a ring under addition and composition, with identity $\id_V$ (Proposition [5.1.5](/notes/math-55a/5-1-linear-maps#proposition-5-1-5)). Composition is also compatible with scalars, $(\lambda\varphi) \circ \psi = \lambda(\varphi \circ \psi) = \varphi \circ (\lambda\psi)$; one says that $\End(V)$ is a $k$-*algebra*. For $\dim V = n$, choosing a basis gives a ring isomorphism $\End(V) \cong \mcM_{n \times n}(k)$ (Corollary [5.2.10](/notes/math-55a/5-2-matrices-of-linear-maps#corollary-5-2-10)), and the ring is noncommutative once $n \geq 2$.

Since endomorphisms can be composed, we can form powers and evaluate polynomials.

:::definition{7.2.1} Powers and polynomials of operators
For $\varphi \in \End(V)$ and $n \in \ZZ_{\geq 0}$: $$\varphi^0 = \id_V, \quad \varphi^n = \underbrace{\varphi \circ \varphi \circ \cdots \circ \varphi}_{n \text{ times}}.$$ For a polynomial $p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n \in k[x]$, define $$p(\varphi) = a_0 \id_V + a_1 \varphi + \cdots + a_n \varphi^n \in \End(V).$$ For $\lambda \in k$ we often write $\varphi - \lambda$ for $\varphi - \lambda\id_V$.
:::

:::proposition{7.2.2} Evaluation homomorphism
The map $\ev_\varphi : k[x] \to \End(V)$ defined by $p(x) \mapsto p(\varphi)$ is a ring homomorphism. That is:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $(p + q)(\varphi) = p(\varphi) + q(\varphi)$.
2. $(pq)(\varphi) = p(\varphi) \circ q(\varphi)$.
3. $1(\varphi) = \id_V$.

In particular, $p(\varphi) \circ q(\varphi) = q(\varphi) \circ p(\varphi)$ for all $p, q \in k[x]$: polynomials in the same operator commute.
:::

:::proof
(a) and (c) are immediate. For (b), let $p(x) = \sum a_i x^i$ and $q(x) = \sum b_j x^j$. Then $(pq)(x) = \sum_{s} c_s x^s$ where $c_s = \sum_{i+j=s} a_i b_j$. Since $\varphi^i \circ \varphi^j = \varphi^{i+j}$ and composition is bilinear, $$\begin{aligned}
(pq)(\varphi) = \sum_s c_s \varphi^s &= \sum_s \Bigl(\sum_{i+j=s} a_i b_j\Bigr) \varphi^s \\
&= \Bigl(\sum_i a_i \varphi^i\Bigr) \circ \Bigl(\sum_j b_j \varphi^j\Bigr) = p(\varphi) \circ q(\varphi).
\end{aligned}$$ The last sentence follows from (b) because $pq = qp$ in $k[x]$.
:::

:::note
A factorization of a polynomial therefore gives a factorization of the operator: if $p(x) = c(x - \lambda_1)\cdots(x - \lambda_d)$, then $p(\varphi) = c(\varphi - \lambda_1)\circ\cdots\circ(\varphi - \lambda_d)$, with the factors in any order. In the language of Chapter 10, the rule $p \cdot v = p(\varphi)(v)$ makes $V$ a module over the ring $k[x]$. The polynomials $p$ with $p(\varphi) = 0$ form the kernel of $\ev_\varphi$; in Section [7.9](/notes/math-55a/7-9-the-cayley-hamilton-theorem-and-the-minimal-polynomial) we show that they are exactly the multiples of a single monic polynomial, the *minimal polynomial* of $\varphi$.
:::
